_comment: The DOCUMENT + IMAGE metadata layer (WebPivot/tools/wp_docmeta.py). A scam site's hosted PDFs (the 'licence', 'certificate', 'prospectus', 'whitepaper') and its own photographs are usually produced on the operator's machine and uploaded untouched — so they carry an Author, a Creator tool, an XMP DocumentID, a camera model, sometimes GPS. Those survive every re-skin of the site itself, because nobody re-exports the PDF when they change the brand. This file decides WHICH files are worth downloading, HOW MUCH bandwidth that may cost, and — most importantly — which metadata values are too GENERIC to cluster on. That last part is the base-rate discipline: 'Microsoft Word' as a Producer is shared by half the internet and is noise; a Producer nobody else uses is a fingerprint. Add a value to a generic_* list and it stops producing same-operator edges (it is still recorded, just demoted to context).

document_extensions._comment: File types downloaded and parsed for embedded document metadata. PDFs are the highest-value target by far: /Info and the XMP packet routinely name the author, the machine's software stack and a per-document UUID. Office formats are listed because they are equally rich (docProps/core.xml), and are parsed when the optional accelerator is available.

image_extensions._comment: Image types downloaded and parsed for EXIF / XMP / PNG-text metadata. A photograph the operator took themselves (an 'office' shot, a team page, a fake KYC prop) can carry camera Make/Model, Artist, Copyright and GPS coordinates. Screenshots and exported graphics instead carry the editing Software, which clusters the shop that made them.

generic_producers._comment: PDF /Producer and /Creator values so common they identify a TOOL, not an operator — the base-rate trap. Matched case-insensitively as a substring, so 'Microsoft' catches every Word build number. A value matching here is still recorded in the artifacts (it is real context: a browser-printed PDF tells you the document was made from a web page) but it will NOT emit a same-operator pivot. Add anything you see across unrelated cases.

generic_software._comment: Image EXIF `Software` / XMP `CreatorTool` values that name a common editor rather than an operator. Same rule as generic_producers: recorded, but never clustered on alone. A NON-generic value here is worth a look — an obscure or CJK-localised editor build narrows the shop considerably.

role_authors._comment: Author / Artist / Creator values that are a DEFAULT rather than a person — the OS account name of a stock image, a shared workstation, or a placeholder the operator never changed. Clustering on these fuses unrelated cases: thousands of documents worldwide are authored by 'Windows User'. Matched case-insensitively against the whole trimmed value, not as a substring, so a real person named e.g. 'Admin Nguyen' is not lost.

skip_path_hints._comment: URL path fragments whose files are framework/CDN/theme assets rather than the operator's own uploads — downloading them costs bandwidth and yields the theme vendor's metadata, which clusters the THEME and not the operator. Matched case-insensitively anywhere in the URL path.

budget._comment: Download limits. This layer FETCHES FILES FROM THE TARGET, so it is a real footprint on the operator's server and a real cost in time — these caps keep it proportionate. max_files is the total downloaded per page; max_bytes_per_file skips anything larger (checked via Content-Length before the body is read); max_total_bytes is the whole-run ceiling; min_image_bytes skips tracking pixels, spacers and icons, which never carry useful metadata. max_documents reserves part of max_files for PDFs/Office files, so a page full of images cannot starve the highest-value target.
